summary: EXOTERRAIN is an interactive web tool that helps find Earth locations that could serve as test sites for Mars terrain. It answers NASA's challenge "Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars". We took 40 km x 40 km windows of real elevation data around Jezero crater on Mars and five Earth sites (Utah desert, Atacama Desert, Mauna Loa, Craters of the Moon and Death Valley), using NASA SRTM data and the NASA MOLA / ESA HRSC blended Mars elevation model. A Python script calculates mean slope, slope variability and local relief for each area. The app then ranks the Earth sites by similarity to the Mars target, lets users change how much each measure counts, and explains why each site ranked as it did. It matters because early field tests on Earth cost far less than testing hardware in space, and open data makes this comparison possible for students and researchers. The tool shows terrain similarity only. It does not claim that any site is suitable for a mission.
details:
What it does
EXOTERRAIN is an interactive web tool that compares the terrain of a target region on Mars (Jezero crater) with Earth locations that could serve as test sites. It computes three terrain measures for each area: mean slope, slope variability, and local relief. The tool uses these to rank the Earth areas by similarity to the target. Users choose the target and which measures count. They can adjust the weight of each measure and see the ranking change. They can also click any area on the map or ranking list to see a side-by-side metric table and a plain-language explanation of why it ranked where it did.

How it works

  1. We took 40 km × 40 km windows of real elevation data around the Mars target and five Earth sites (Utah desert, Chile’s Atacama Desert, Mauna Loa in Hawaii, Craters of the Moon in Idaho, and Death Valley).
  2. Both sides were resampled to similar cell sizes of about 150–200 m, so the comparison is fair.
  3. A Python script (compute_metrics.py) calculates slope from the elevation grids and writes the results to a CSV file, plus a log of every data source and access date.
  4. The app standardizes each measure to a 0–1 scale across the loaded areas, calculates a weighted distance to the target, and converts it into a 0–100 similarity score.
  5. A sensitivity check shows whether the top pick stays first when the weights change or a measure is dropped.

Data used

  • Earth: NASA SRTM 1 arc-second elevation (about 30 m), via the open Terrain Tiles dataset.
  • Mars: USGS MOLA–HRSC blended global elevation model at 200 m, built from NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor MOLA instrument and ESA’s Mars Express HRSC camera.

Benefits and intended impact
The tool makes planetary terrain data easier for students, educators and researchers to explore. It could help with early thinking about where field tests might be done on Earth before hardware goes to Mars. Every number is traceable to a named dataset, so the result can be checked.

Tools

  • Languages and libraries: Python (NumPy, rasterio), HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Platforms: Google Colab for data processing, GitHub for code hosting, GitHub Pages for the live app
  • Hardware: laptops and phones

What is creative about it
The tool avoids a black-box “AI match”. The score is simple and visible, and users can change the weights themselves and watch the ranking move. It also compares Earth and Mars with the same derived terrain measures, rather than raw elevations, which are not comparable across planets.

What we considered

  • Earth and Mars have different gravity, atmosphere, geology and reference surfaces, so we compared only terrain shape.
  • Data resolution and window size can change slope values, so we matched them as closely as possible.
  • SRTM only covers 56°S to 60°N, which limited the Earth sites we could choose.
  • The ranking is a prototype score, not a scientific probability. It does not assess dust, temperature, radiation, soil, atmosphere or safety, and it does not say a site is suitable for a mission.
dataRefs: NASA SRTM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) elevation data
